newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government steps in to truckers' dispute.
newsitem.headline: French government steps in to truckers' dispute.

text.p: The French government stepped in to a truckers dispute on Sunday, picking a mediator to help end seven-day blockades of many towns and petrol depots across the country.
Unions urged truckers, pressing for shorter working hours, wage hikes and retirement at 55 instead of 60, to hold fast.

After the third round of talks failed late on Saturday, union officials said that the nomination by Transport Minister Bernard Pons would be followed immediately by new negotiations with haulage bosses.

Pons had met union chiefs late on Saturday, intervening directly for the first time in a dispute which echoes a damaging 24-day rail strike a year ago which sent Prime Minister Alain Juppe's popularity plummeting.
Unions welcomed the proposal but several threatened to harden the protest, which is weighing on the economy, if the mediator failed to obtain quick results.
"If there is progress on Sunday, we don't rule out the possibility of spreading the movement to (school and other bus services)," Claude Debons of the pro-Socialist CFDT union said.
Debons told reporters he was not certain the mediator would be able to engineer a rapid solution because the haulage bosses were refusing to make concessions.
CFDT leader Nicole Notat had on Friday called for a truckers' demonstration in Paris on Monday if talks failed to break the deadlock.
The Force Ouvriere union was more optimistic, saying that Pons was willing to help fund retirement at 55 but only as part of a general agreement solving the dispute.
The haulage companies said in a statement that they had made as many concessions as they could, including retirement at 55 and full payment of all working hours, including time spent loading.

Tens of thousands of trucks blocked main roads around some 30 cities and a dozen fuel depots. Some blockades were eased but unions said this was only to give strikers a weekend break, and the screw would be tightened once again from later on Sunday.
The southwest, parts of the south and the Calvados region in Normandy were all badly hit.
Petrol stations have run out of fuel in areas of Normandy and the south-west around Bordeaux, the city where Juppe is mayor and singled out for the toughest protests.
"People are panicking, they're rushing to fill up their cars. Some are piling up jerrycans in their cars," said the owner of a petrol station in Marseille.
But in other areas including the north and the Paris region there was little risk of shortages.

Several dozen truckers have blocked a motorway close to Paris's wholesale food market at Rungis but unions said they did not plan to seal off the market which handles two million tonnes of food supplies a day.

On the ring-road around Caen in Normandy, two people died and four were injured on Saturday evening when a car rammed a lorry which had been blockading the motorway. Police said the car had apparently skirted barriers sealing the road off.

Thousands of foreign truckers, most British and Spanish with no alternative but to drive through France, became stranded in the roadblocks, many sleeping in their cabs and running out of food and money.
More than 1,000 British truck drivers were stuck in blockades across France and British freight operators said the dispute was ruining them.
